title: Quantization profiles technical deep dive (route-level enablement) - Acme AI x Redwood
summary: Acme AI reviewed Redwood’s opt-in Quantization Profile Library and asked detailed questions about (a) route-level enablement semantics (per route + optional region/tier), (b) determinism and “no silent changes” guarantees, (c) compatibility checks (GPU SKU / max context / model variant) and fallback behavior, (d) quality guardrails and regression thresholds, and (e) rollback mechanics (route-level disable + global kill switch) including audit logs/RBAC. Redwood confirmed v1 uses explicit profile references (versioned) with safe fallback to baseline precision when incompatible, plus observability signals (applied vs fallback) and a staged rollout plan with canaries and offline eval gating. Next steps: Redwood to share draft docs + compatibility matrix and set up a short follow-up on security/change control; Acme to provide target routes/models and traffic profile for initial beta design partner scope.
topics: Quality eval suites, thresholds, and rollout gates
Audit logs, RBAC, and change control expectations
action_items: Markus Klein (Redwood) - Send Acme the route-level enablement doc + API examples and clarify explicit profile_ref vs alias behavior - 2025-02-07
Arjun Desai (Redwood) - Share the quality guardrails summary (required eval suites + acceptable deltas) and recommended A/B evaluation playbook - 2025-02-10
Noah Patel (Redwood) - Provide notes on determinism + runtime signals (quant_profile_id annotation, applied/fallback) and any known KV cache caveats - 2025-02-10
Chloe Martin (Redwood) - Confirm Console workflow: warnings, compatibility preview, audit trail fields visible to customer admins - 2025-02-12
Sarah Chen (Acme AI) - Send Redwood the shortlist of models/routes to target for beta, plus GPU types/regions and max context usage - 2025-02-11
Tom Alvarez (Acme AI) - Share Acme change-control requirements (approvals, audit export fields, retention) for route config changes - 2025-02-14
next_steps: Redwood to email a short packet: schema overview, enablement API/Console screenshots (or mock), rollback runbook excerpt, and current compatibility matrix draft.
Acme to confirm whether beta should start on Hosted API or Dedicated capacity (and which region).
Schedule a 30-min security/change-control follow-up (Acme security + Redwood platform/security) to cover RBAC and audit export fields.
Schedule a 45-min working session to pick one route for a 1% canary and define success metrics (cost/token, p95 latency, quality delta).
transcript:
Meeting: Quantization profiles technical deep dive (route-level enablement) - Acme AI x Redwood
Date: 2025-02-06
Start time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 min

Attendees
- Redwood: Markus Klein, Arjun Desai, Noah Patel, Chloe Martin
- Acme AI: Sarah Chen, David Kim, Nina Rao, Tom Alvarez


[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for jumping on. This is the technical deep dive we talked about for the quantization profile library, specifically route-level enablement. We’ll keep it pretty concrete: what knobs exist, what’s deterministic, and how rollback works.

[00:17] Sarah Chen: Sounds good. We’ve been looking for ways to cut cost without doing a full self-hosted vLLM thing. But we’re… cautious on quality changes.

[00:26] Markus Klein: Yep. That’s exactly why we’re doing opt-in and per route. Arjun and Noah are here to go deep on profiles + runtime, and Chloe can cover the control plane / Console bits.

[00:38] David Kim: Great. We read the high-level note, but we want to understand: is the toggle like “quantization on/off” or do we pick a specific profile?

[00:47] Chloe Martin: For v1 it’s “pick a specific profile reference” or leave it as default. Default means no change from current serving precision. The route config can point to a profile, and we validate it before it becomes active.

[01:01] David Kim: So it’s not like ‘latest recommended’ that can change under us?

[01:05] Markus Klein: Good question. The direction is: no silent changes. We’ve debated aliases like “recommended” but we’re leaning that if we ever offer it, it’s explicit and comes with change notifications. For the beta, it’s versioned profile refs.

[01:20] Sarah Chen: Okay. And “route” in your world is the endpoint we define, right? Like /summarize uses model X, /chat uses model Y?

[01:27] Chloe Martin: Exactly. Route is the unit where you set model, max tokens, safety stuff, and now quantization profile. And optionally scoping by region or deployment tier, depending on what you’re using.

[01:41] Nina Rao: When you say region/tier: we run mostly us-east and eu-west. Could we enable in us-east first only?

[01:48] Chloe Martin: Yes. The policy layer can resolve “route config + region + deployment mode” and return the profile to apply. We can do that for canary.

[02:00] Noah Patel: And from runtime side, we treat the resolved profile as part of the execution plan. We annotate the request with the profile id we actually applied, or whether we fell back.

[02:11] David Kim: Let’s dig into fallback. If the profile is incompatible with the hardware, what happens? Does it error? Or it runs baseline?

[02:19] Noah Patel: It should not hard error for incompatibility. The safe behavior is baseline precision. You’ll see a “fallback_reason” in metrics. We do error only if something’s wrong like corrupted artifact, but even then we have a global kill switch and route disable.

[02:37] Tom Alvarez: That’s a big deal for us. We cannot have user requests failing because someone toggled a cost knob.

[02:43] Markus Klein: Totally understood. The whole philosophy is “degrade safely.”

[02:49] Sarah Chen: But if it silently falls back, aren’t we thinking we’re getting savings when we’re not?

[02:54] Noah Patel: Right, so we make it very visible. There’s an “applied_rate” vs “fallback_rate” metric. And per request you’ll see the quant_profile_id tag in traces/logs.

[03:06] Nina Rao: How do we check for a single request? Like, we have a request ID from our logs.

[03:12] Chloe Martin: In Console there’s a request explorer where you paste the request id, and it shows route resolution. At least that’s what we’re building. Today we can do it via trace search.

[03:23] Markus Klein: We can show you a mock after this.

[03:26] David Kim: Let’s step back to the profile itself. Arjun, what’s inside one of these profiles? Is it like int8 weights, fp16 activations, that kind of thing?

[03:36] Arjun Desai: Yeah. Think of it as a bundle: quant method (like INT8 weight-only or FP8 mix depending on model), calibration set reference, any caveats, and importantly constraints: which model variant, max context length range, and which GPU classes it’s been validated on.

[03:58] Sarah Chen: Constraints include sequence length? Because our chat route can hit 16k context sometimes.

[04:04] Arjun Desai: Yes. We’ve seen profiles behave differently at long contexts, sometimes quality drift, sometimes latency changes. So profiles declare max_context or “validated_up_to.” The policy engine uses that.

[04:20] David Kim: Wait, the policy engine knows the request’s context length before running?

[04:25] Noah Patel: We know the requested max tokens and we can see prompt length tokens after tokenization. There are some nuances with streaming and tool calls, but for gating we mostly use prompt length and route-level max context.

[04:41] David Kim: Okay. That’s good.

[04:44] Tom Alvarez: I’m going to ask the compliance-ish question. Who can enable this? Is it behind admin only?

[04:51] Chloe Martin: It’s behind RBAC. Route config changes require “Route Admin” permissions in Console or via API tokens with that scope. Every change emits an audit event with actor, time, route, and diff.

[05:07] Tom Alvarez: Can we export those audit events? We have a SIEM.

[05:11] Markus Klein: Yes, audit logs export is part of our enterprise package. We can confirm the exact fields, but it includes route id, previous profile ref, new profile ref, and if kill switch was toggled.

[05:26] Sarah Chen: On the “kill switch,” is that global across tenant? Or global across Redwood?

[05:31] Chloe Martin: Both concepts exist. There’s an emergency global disable at the platform level, and we’re also adding a tenant-level override to disable all profiles if needed. For you, the relevant one is tenant override plus route-level disable.

[05:48] Nina Rao: So if we detect a regression, we can disable within minutes?

[05:52] Markus Klein: Yeah, that’s the goal. Route-level disable is a config change. Propagation depends on caching but it’s designed to be fast—minutes, not hours.

[06:04] David Kim: What about cached profile metadata? I’m worried about thundering herd if every request checks profile.

[06:10] Noah Patel: We don’t fetch per request. Route resolution is cached. Profile artifacts are loaded on worker init or when the resolved profile changes. We also rate-limit metadata fetches to protect the registry.

[06:27] David Kim: Okay. Good.

[06:29] Sarah Chen: On quality: what is the gating? Like what stops us from enabling a profile that passes your internal eval but breaks our domain?

[06:39] Arjun Desai: Great point. Our guardrails have two layers. One: Redwood’s standard prompt sets / eval suites per model family. If a profile doesn’t meet thresholds, it won’t be publishable. Two: we strongly recommend you run your own A/B eval on a slice of your real traffic or your internal test set before scaling beyond a small canary.

[07:03] Sarah Chen: What are the thresholds? “No regression” is vague.

[07:08] Arjun Desai: It’s not zero. It’s per task family. Like summarization has tighter tolerance on factuality metrics, and some creative chat has slightly wider. We use statistical tests and block if it’s beyond threshold with confidence. I can send the exact policy doc.

[07:27] Nina Rao: What metrics do you use? BLEU isn’t useful for our stuff.

[07:31] Arjun Desai: Yeah, we don’t rely on BLEU. We use task-specific graders, LLM-as-judge with calibrations, and some reference-based checks where applicable. Plus safety regressions. It’s a mix. The key is we don’t ship profiles that fail the baseline suites.

[07:52] David Kim: But there’s a risk you change the profile over time. Like v2 of a profile.

[07:57] Markus Klein: Which is why versioning is explicit. “profile_id: foo@1.2.0” kind of thing. If we publish 1.3.0, you don’t get it unless you change the ref.

[08:09] Sarah Chen: Okay. That’s critical. We had issues with a provider updating something and it changed outputs.

[08:16] Noah Patel: Also runtime selection is deterministic given (model version, profile version, hardware). We don’t do “best effort” kernel guessing without guardrails. Hiro isn’t on the call but that’s the focus.

[08:31] David Kim: Deterministic meaning same input -> same output?

[08:35] Noah Patel: I’ll be careful: LLMs are stochastic if temperature > 0. Deterministic in terms of config resolution and quant mode. I mean: the same request under same route config resolves to same profile and same kernel path, no flapping.

[08:53] David Kim: Got it.

[08:55] Sarah Chen: Let’s talk about model coverage. We use Llama 3.1 70B for our main assistant and also some smaller rerank model.

[09:03] Arjun Desai: For v1 we’re targeting the common open models first. Llama 3.x variants are on the list. For rerank/embeddings it’s a bit different; weight-only INT8 might apply, but we’re prioritizing generation.

[09:20] Nina Rao: Are profiles per GPU? We run A100 on dedicated, but sometimes H100 when we burst.

[09:28] Arjun Desai: Profiles declare compatible hardware classes. Some methods are A100-friendly, some are really only good on H100 due to FP8 tensor cores. So you can have separate profiles or just a profile that’s constrained.

[09:44] Chloe Martin: And if you have a route that can land on either A100 or H100 pools, policy will apply only when compatible; otherwise fallback.

[09:54] Sarah Chen: So in that case, savings are inconsistent.

[09:57] Markus Klein: Correct, unless you pin the route to a tier/pool. For predictable savings, we recommend dedicated pools or a route policy that targets a compatible SKU.

[10:09] David Kim: Does the Console show expected impact? Like “this will save 20% cost but may increase latency”?

[10:16] Chloe Martin: We’re adding “expected deltas” based on our perf benchmarks. It’s not a guarantee, but it’s directional. And we’ll show “validated on GPU: A100/H100” and “validated up to context: 8k” etc.

[10:35] Tom Alvarez: Does it show warnings? Like “experimental.”

[10:38] Chloe Martin: Yes. Profiles can be marked experimental or deprecated, and we surface that. Enabling a deprecated one is blocked.

[10:49] Sarah Chen: Can you talk about rollback in more detail? Say we canary 1% and quality drops.

[10:55] Markus Klein: There are three levers: (1) disable the profile on that route (set it back to default), (2) if you accidentally enabled in multiple routes, tenant-level disable, and (3) platform kill switch in a true emergency.

[11:10] Noah Patel: And in runtime, if kill switch is on, we ignore profile refs entirely and run baseline.

[11:17] David Kim: Is there any risk of a fallback loop? Like it tries profile, fails, tries again.

[11:23] Noah Patel: There was an edge case early where policy re-evaluated weirdly, but it’s fixed. The resolution is “apply OR fallback,” and that’s final for the request.

[11:35] Sarah Chen: Okay.

[11:37] Nina Rao: What’s the timeline for beta?

[11:41] Markus Klein: We’re aiming to start with 2-3 design partners in the next few weeks. That’s why we’re talking. If you’re interested, we’d define one route, one model variant, one region, and start with a tiny canary.

[11:57] Sarah Chen: We are interested. But we need strong audit / change control.

[12:01] Tom Alvarez: And we need to know the data plane doesn’t send prompts anywhere new because of this. Like calibration data.

[12:08] Arjun Desai: Calibration sets are internal. Your prompts are not used for calibration unless you explicitly opt into a separate program, which is not part of this. Profiles are precomputed artifacts.

[12:21] Tom Alvarez: Okay.

[12:23] David Kim: One more: caching. We use long system prompts. If quantization changes KV cache behavior, can it cause memory issues or latency spikes?

[12:34] Noah Patel: Great question. Some profiles change memory footprint a bit. We validate VRAM and cache interactions in a perf suite. But you’re right, certain quant modes can change KV cache layout or kernel selection, and we’ve seen decode latency regressions in a couple combos. That’s why we gate by GPU and context and we keep a clear rollback.

[12:59] Sarah Chen: So it’s not always a free lunch.

[13:01] Noah Patel: Exactly. Typically cost/token down, sometimes latency slightly up or down depending on kernel. We measure p95 and tail.

[13:11] Nina Rao: Would this work on Dedicated? We care about predictable throughput.

[13:16] Markus Klein: Yes, Hosted and Dedicated are both in scope. Dedicated is actually easier for consistency because you know the GPU.

[13:26] David Kim: We’re also using function calling. Any risk quant changes break structured outputs?

[13:33] Arjun Desai: Quantization can affect output distribution, so structured output compliance can shift. We run structured-output evals in the harness, and we recommend you test your tool-calling flows specifically. In beta, we’ll help set up those checks.

[13:54] Sarah Chen: What’s the actual API change? Is it a new field in route config?

[13:58] Chloe Martin: Yes, a field like quantization_profile_ref. If absent or set to “default,” nothing changes. If set, it references a profile id in the library.

[14:12] David Kim: Can we set it via SDK? We mostly use Python.

[14:15] Chloe Martin: Yes, we’ll have SDK support. Worst case in beta you can hit the REST endpoint.

[14:23] Markus Klein: Monica from SDK isn’t here, but we can share examples.

[14:28] Sarah Chen: Okay.

[14:30] Tom Alvarez: On approvals: do you support a two-person rule? Like, someone proposes and another approves.

[14:37] Chloe Martin: Not in v1 as a first-class workflow. We do have audit logs + RBAC, and we can restrict who can write changes. Some customers implement approvals in their own CI pipeline using the config API.

[14:55] Tom Alvarez: That might be okay if audit is strong.

[14:58] Markus Klein: We can walk through patterns we’ve seen.

[15:02] Sarah Chen: Let’s talk about “recommended.” You said no silent changes. But is there any plan where Redwood updates a recommended profile under the hood?

[15:11] Markus Klein: For v1: no. For future: if we add “recommended,” the plan is it’s an alias that points to a version, and you can subscribe to notifications. But we’re not doing “we flip it and your outputs change.”

[15:26] David Kim: Great.

[15:27] Nina Rao: How do we validate compatibility before enabling? Like, can we get a dry run?

[15:33] Chloe Martin: In Console, when you select a profile, we show a compatibility preview: it checks your route’s model variant, the region/tier, max context settings, and your account’s allowed deployments. API returns detailed errors if not compatible.

[15:52] Nina Rao: Good.

[15:54] Sarah Chen: What about model version pinning? We pin model versions for weeks.

[16:00] Chloe Martin: Works fine. Profiles are also tied to model variant + version, so if you change model version, the same profile may be incompatible; we’d warn you.

[16:13] Noah Patel: And runtime uses the exact model hash + profile id. If mismatch, it won’t apply.

[16:21] David Kim: Okay.

[16:23] Markus Klein: Maybe we can go into what the rollout would look like with you. Sarah, what’s the route you’d start with?

[16:30] Sarah Chen: Probably summarization. It’s high volume but less safety-sensitive than chat. We do, like, customer support case summaries.

[16:39] Nina Rao: It’s also shorter contexts usually, under 4k.

[16:43] Arjun Desai: That’s a good candidate. We have strong eval coverage for summarization.

[16:49] David Kim: But we care about factuality. If it hallucinates, that’s bad.

[16:53] Arjun Desai: Understood. We can add your domain prompt set into the A/B harness. We do paired comparisons baseline vs quant, then look at factuality graders and human spot checks.

[17:10] Sarah Chen: How do you run A/B? Is it at request time, shadow?

[17:15] Arjun Desai: Typically we sample from production logs (with your consent and privacy settings) or you provide a dataset. Then we run offline. For online canary, we route 1% to quantized and compare aggregate metrics plus targeted evaluations.

[17:35] Nina Rao: If it’s online, do we need to do deterministic sampling? So the same user stays on one variant?

[17:41] Chloe Martin: The routing system supports consistent hashing if you want stickiness by user/session. For early canary we usually just do random per request, but we can discuss.

[17:55] David Kim: For our support workflows, consistency is good. But maybe not required at 1%.

[18:01] Sarah Chen: Okay.

[18:03] Tom Alvarez: I want to know: do you log “profile applied” in audit logs or in runtime logs? Different thing.

[18:10] Noah Patel: Runtime logs and traces. Audit log is config changes. For runtime, we emit a metric and annotate traces with quant_profile_id and a result like applied/fallback/disabled.

[18:24] Tom Alvarez: Perfect.

[18:25] Markus Klein: Also, if you’re on Dedicated, we can set alerts on fallback_rate. If it spikes, that means something is off.

[18:35] Nina Rao: What would cause fallback_rate to spike besides incompatibility?

[18:39] Chloe Martin: Common causes: route moved to a different GPU pool, region shift, or someone changed max context. Or a profile got deprecated/blocked, but then the UI/API would warn.

[18:55] Sarah Chen: Deprecation means you can yank a profile?

[18:58] Markus Klein: If we detect a severe regression, we may block new enables and recommend disabling. For already-enabled routes, we try not to force-change, but in extreme cases we may use the platform kill switch or policy blocklist. That’s rare and we’d communicate.

[19:17] David Kim: That’s the “no silent changes” tension.

[19:20] Markus Klein: Yes. The principle is: we don’t change your config. But we will protect platform reliability. If a profile is actively causing failures, we may have to block it. We’ll have a runbook and comms.

[19:35] Sarah Chen: That’s acceptable if it’s safety.

[19:38] Nina Rao: For cost savings, what’s typical? Like percent.

[19:43] Arjun Desai: Depends on model and GPU. For certain 70B class on A100, weight-only INT8 can be meaningful. For H100 FP8 paths, can be bigger. I don’t want to promise a number on the call, but we can share benchmark deltas for the specific model.

[20:05] David Kim: Latency impact?

[20:07] Noah Patel: Also workload-dependent. Decode heavy vs prefill heavy. Sometimes prefill improves, sometimes decode gets worse if kernel isn’t ideal. That’s why we do the perf suite.

[20:23] Sarah Chen: So we should expect to test both cost and p95 latency.

[20:26] Markus Klein: Yes.

[20:28] Tom Alvarez: Are there any security implications of the profile artifacts? Where stored?

[20:33] Chloe Martin: Stored in our model registry artifact store, signed, and fetched by runtime through internal auth. For Private deployments, you can host artifacts in your environment. For Hosted/Dedicated it’s within Redwood.

[20:51] Tom Alvarez: Signed is good.

[20:53] David Kim: Quick question: does profile selection happen in the router or in the runtime?

[20:59] Chloe Martin: The control plane resolves the policy and returns “resolved profile ref” to the runtime. Router enforces high-level constraints, runtime applies.

[21:09] Noah Patel: Exactly. Runtime doesn’t do a bunch of logic; it receives resolved config and checks again for safety.

[21:17] David Kim: Double validation.

[21:18] Noah Patel: Yeah.

[21:20] Sarah Chen: Okay, I think we have the core. Can we talk about what we need to do to be a design partner?

[21:26] Markus Klein: Sure. Usually we pick: one route, one model variant, one region. You agree to run the eval harness with us and do a staged rollout: 0% -> 1% -> 10% -> 50% if all good.

[21:43] Nina Rao: We can do that. We need some automation though.

[21:46] Chloe Martin: We can do config changes via API, so you can tie it to your deployment pipeline.

[21:53] David Kim: We’ll need the exact endpoint docs.

[21:56] Markus Klein: We’ll send them.

[22:00] Sarah Chen: And for Dedicated, do we need to change anything? Like new image.

[22:05] Noah Patel: There may be a runtime build version requirement because the quant profile loading needs support. If you’re on our managed Dedicated, we can schedule it.

[22:18] Sarah Chen: Okay.

[22:19] Tom Alvarez: If we go to production, we want an SLA around rollback. Like, if we ask to disable, it happens quickly.

[22:27] Markus Klein: We can discuss operational expectations. For beta we’ll be pretty hands-on. For GA, it’s self-serve with a documented rollback process.

[22:39] Nina Rao: What about observability dashboards? Do we get a panel showing “enabled routes” and “fallback rate”?

[22:45] Chloe Martin: Yes, that’s part of it. We’ll show route-level metrics with filters by model and region.

[22:54] David Kim: I’d like to see example metric names. We have Grafana.

[22:58] Noah Patel: We can share. It’s something like quant_profile_applied_total and quant_profile_fallback_total, plus tags.

[23:10] Sarah Chen: Okay.

[23:12] Markus Klein: Anything else you’re worried about that we didn’t cover?

[23:16] David Kim: Potentially: if we set the profile in the route config, does that affect all clients hitting the route? Like internal vs external.

[23:24] Chloe Martin: Yes, it’s route-level. If you need segmentation, we can create two routes or use routing rules.

[23:33] Sarah Chen: We can do two routes. That’s fine.

[23:36] Tom Alvarez: On audit logs: we need actor identity. Is it tied to SSO?

[23:42] Chloe Martin: If you have SSO/SAML enabled, yes, actor is the user identity. If it’s API token, it logs token name + owning service account.

[23:55] Tom Alvarez: Perfect.

[23:56] Nina Rao: I have a practical question: how do we revert fast if Console is down? Like incident.

[24:02] Chloe Martin: You can revert via API as well. And SRE can toggle the tenant override if needed.

[24:10] Markus Klein: Also the kill switch is managed by Redwood SRE, not customers, but we can act if necessary.

[24:17] Sarah Chen: Okay.

[24:19] Arjun Desai: One thing I want to mention: some profiles will be labeled “experimental.” For design partners we might start there, but we’ll be transparent.

[24:29] Sarah Chen: As long as it’s opt-in and scoped, it’s okay.

[24:33] Markus Klein: Great.

[24:34] (crosstalk)
[24:35] David Kim: Sorry, one more—does enabling quant change cost reporting? Like will we see the cost delta per route?

[24:42] Markus Klein: Yes, we attribute cost/token per route and you can compare before/after. Nadia on our side owns some of that, but the dashboard will show it.

[24:53] David Kim: Good.

[24:55] Sarah Chen: Alright. Next steps wise, can you send the docs packet and we’ll identify a route and model.

[25:02] Markus Klein: Yep. I’ll send: schema overview, enablement API, rollback runbook excerpt, and a compatibility matrix draft.

[25:12] Arjun Desai: I’ll add the eval policy and the A/B playbook. It’ll probably be a PDF or a doc link.

[25:19] Noah Patel: I’ll include runtime notes on determinism and the trace tags.

[25:24] Chloe Martin: And I’ll confirm the Console workflow and what’s visible in audit history.

[25:30] Sarah Chen: Great.

[25:32] Tom Alvarez: Can we schedule a security follow-up? 30 minutes.

[25:36] Markus Klein: Absolutely. We’ll loop in our security engineering and platform folks.

[25:42] Nina Rao: And then a working session with our engineers to set up the canary.

[25:46] Markus Klein: Yep. We’ll propose times.

[25:49] Sarah Chen: Okay, thanks everyone.

[25:52] Markus Klein: Thank you. We’ll follow up over email.

[25:56] (meeting continues with brief scheduling chatter; transcription ends early due to call wrap-up)
